# Amara's Vigil

Amara was thirty-four when armed men entered the safe house in Lagos where she had been sheltering with her sister. She had been there for three days, waiting for papers that would allow them to leave the country. The men came in the evening, moving through the rooms with methodical purpose. What followed was not a single violent moment but a prolonged ordeal—hours of interrogation, of being restrained, of pain applied with deliberate precision to her arms and torso. They wanted information about her husband's political activities. She gave them nothing because she knew nothing, but they did not believe her. The worst part, in some ways, was the silence between the sessions of questioning—the waiting in a locked room, not knowing when they would return, what they would do next, her body braced for what was coming. She escaped two days later when a guard made an error. She and her sister made their way to the American embassy, and within six months Amara was living in Philadelphia with her husband, who had fled months earlier. By all external measures, she had survived. She was alive. She was safe. But now, at forty-two, eight years after those three days in Lagos, she carried the trauma with her like a second body.

The triggers had emerged gradually, then settled into a pattern that governed her waking life. Silence was the most disorienting—not the absence of sound itself, but the sudden cessation of it. When the train she conducted pulled into a station and the engines cut, when she woke at three in the morning to find the house absolutely still, when a passenger's conversation ended abruptly, Amara's nervous system flooded with the certainty that someone was coming. She had come to dread the quiet moments that other people found restful. Any visible injury on another person—a bandaged hand, a cut on someone's face, even a bruise—yanked her backward into the locked room, her body responding as though witnessing the violence that had been inflicted on her. And smoke, the smell of it, sent her into a state of vigilant terror that lasted hours, though she could not articulate why. She had also begun to notice that certain times of day triggered a nameless dread—evening hours especially, when the light faded, when the world outside the train windows grew dark.

Her body had become a surveillance system. Amara checked herself constantly—running her hands over her arms, her ribs, her legs, searching for signs of injury or threat. It was an exhausting inventory that never yielded reassurance. She had taken up smoking herself, a habit she had quit twenty years ago, because the act of smoking gave her hands something to do and created a barrier of familiar scent between herself and the world. She spent hours mentally rehearsing catastrophes—her home being broken into, her husband being attacked, the train derailing—running through each scenario in meticulous detail, as though thorough preparation could somehow prevent disaster. At work, her hypervigilance had become noticeable to her colleagues. She listened obsessively for sounds that might indicate an intrusion into the conductor's cabin. When passengers moved suddenly—reaching for luggage, standing abruptly from their seats—she went rigid, her entire body locking in readiness. Her supervisor had begun to ask if she was all right. She was not sleeping well. Even on weekends, in her own home with her husband beside her, Amara could not relax. Her mind remained tethered to threat, scanning, waiting, unable to settle into the safety that her rational mind knew was present.

The memories themselves were fragmented and overwhelming. When she tried to recall the event—tried to make sense of it for herself, let alone to tell someone else—she found only images: a man's face looming close, the texture of the wall her cheek was pressed against, a hand reaching toward her. These pictures came without sequence, without the coherence of a story. And when they came, they did not feel like memories at all. They felt like the event happening again, in real time, her body responding as though the danger were present. The distinction between then and now collapsed entirely. Her heart would race, her breathing would shallow, her muscles would tense as if she were still in that locked room, still waiting for the next session of questioning. She could not control when these moments arrived, and they had begun to intrude more frequently into her daily life.

What brought Amara to therapy now, after eight years of managing alone, was a shift at work. The railroad was implementing new safety protocols that required conductors to work in pairs on night routes. The thought of being confined in a small space with another person, unable to control the environment, unable to monitor all entrances and exits, had pushed her to the edge of what she could bear. She had not yet told her husband how afraid she was—how the prospect of those confined night shifts made her feel as though she were being locked away again. Her job, which had once been a source of pride and stability, had become a source of mounting dread. What she wanted most was to feel safe in her own mind again, to move through the world without her nervous system treating every silence as a prelude to violence. What she feared most was that she never would, and that the life she had fought so hard to build would continue to be consumed by the shadow of those three days.
